title: Manifesting Kanzeon
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose emphasizes that true generosity is not about achieving a specific goal, but about cultivating awareness and response to suffering through compassion and mindfulness. By letting go of mental processes and obstacles, we can embody dana in our daily lives, recognizing the interconnectedness of all phenomena and offering genuine support to others without condition or expectation. This approach requires self-care and recognition of one's own limitations, allowing us to receive help when needed and truly offer generosity from a place of openness and receptivity.

sentences.text: This is an honor to be here in Zendo, my first occasion to actually be at the front of the room instead of sitting so wonderfully comfortably and happy in this great space we created.
Good morning.
I'm going to speak this morning about dana in the context of manifesting Kanzeon, kuanyin.
So first of all, an admission.
Over the last number of weeks, including four weeks in Mexico, I've taken some notes and done some readings in preparation for this talk.
Friday night, after getting back from a short trip with friends actually up to Harrison Hot Springs, I sat down to put some order to these thoughts and inadvertently hit a button on my keyboard.
My files disappeared.
And for some reason, the switch for automatic save hadn't been triggered.
So all my notes.
Great lesson and patience.
So I'm going to make this presentation today with some of the thoughts I had in mind to address, but forgive me if at some points there may be some discontinuities, or as they say, leaps of faith.
The realm of Kanzeon and generosity is boundless and timeless, of incomprehensible depth and width.
I will only hint at glints of that light this morning.

I'd like to try to connect some of the thoughts and investigations that [unclear: "Rezola"], [unclear: "Talus"], Ken, Desiree, and Hannah and others have brought to this discussion of the paramitas, with a focus towards dana, or generosity.
We each chose our topics independently and certainly not with any ordered intent.
Ken's comments on Buddha's lists of ten and their inherent inability to linguistically evidence their reflections and interpenetrations is front and center with these six or ten paramitas.

They are certainly not a step-by-step process or hierarchy, but more akin to the image of the net of Indra in which each element reflects the other and illuminates each in multiple ways and directions.

What I'd like to try to do today is connect the idea of dana, the paramita of generosity, with its embodiment in our lives in the framework of our Zen practice through the great bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara.
Two examples here in front of us, one in our Buddha hall.
She, he, because depending on which country, which temple, he can be either or both sexes.

She who sees the suffering of the world, as the exemplary practitioner of prajnaparamita, great wisdom, whom we embrace when we chant, as we just did, the Heart Sutra, and how she so generously offers the dharma and all its embodiments and simultaneously [unclear: "remove those assurances"] to manifest in each of us.
With thanks to Nomon Tim's talk last month on the Heart Sutra, when referencing John Blofield's story, which I then kind of read: this happens early in John Blofield's career, early on in China.
He asked the bodhisattva statue, Kuan Yin statue, if she was real.
And he heard a clear response, and that response was, "Look not for my reality in the realm of appearances or in the void, seek it in your own mind, there only it resides."
How do we recognize, find, and train ourselves to cultivate this and the other perfections in our lives?
Avalokiteshvara, Kannon or Kanzeon in Japanese, or as Kuan Yin in Chinese, is regarded as the mother of all Buddhas.
And in Japan, Kuan Yin is considered to be a Buddha.
We recognize him, her, in our meal chant, as the ninth and final Bodhisattva, Mahasattva, when reciting the Buddha's ten names.
And as [unclear: "Razalit"] reminded us in her introductory talk on Dhanah, when we sit in the lap of the Buddha, there is no separate self.
Sitting in Buddha's lap, Kannon's lap, sitting on our cushion, in the perfection of meditation, Prajnaparamita, there is no separate self, nothing to hold onto.
The inherent generosity of our interconnected beings always provides Oryoki, or just enough.
The name Avalokiteshvara is translated as the one who sees the cries of the world.
She hears all painful cries for help and has the wonderful ability to help all beings in danger and misfortune.
According to one prominent legend, as he was looking down at the suffering of the world, her head literally blew apart from pain of absorbing all that suffering.
And her spiritual father, Amitabha Buddha, put the pieces together of her head as nine new heads.
And his wish to help all beings caused the body to grow a thousand, an immeasurable number of arms, with an eye in the palm of each hand.
And with her many eyes and her hands, each with an instrument of helping, Kanzeon perceives the suffering of all beings and can act to free those suffering beings without limit.
Taigen Dan Leighton, in his primary text Bodhisattva Archetypes, briefly summarizes this vast toolbox.

*Many of the hands hold tools and implements including Dharma wheels, lotuses, Buddhas, jewels embodying the sun and moon, as well as ropes, axes, swords, mirrors, rosaries, vases, [unclear: "conks"], books, willow branches, bows and arrows.

These thousand hands and eyes represent Avalokiteshvara's practice of skillful means, compassionately assisting beings by whatever methods could be effective, using whatever comes to hand as needed at that particular moment.*
So I'd like to begin this presentation with a little story about my personal interaction and relationship with Kanzeon and making him her part of my daily breathing life.

Before I formally started practicing Zen, maybe 14 years ago, I spent a weekend at the San Francisco Zen Center, I spent actually a day at the San Francisco Zen Center, as part of a weekend visit to San Francisco for the first time.
I went over for a Saturday morning tea, and there I met a monk named Joan Amaral who had just completed a seven-year stay at Tassajara.
Hearing my background in farming and construction, she invited me to come to Tassajara.
I had no background or experience of Zen or focused meditation, so when I got home I decided to return to the Zen Center for a few days for a mini residency to see how it felt to practice.
Three things happened during my stay, my four-day stay.
On the first morning, I woke up and, responding to the booming Han, sat for services in the Zendo.
I felt at home, which was a remarkable experience since it was just a little plywood cubby in the basement.

Then, during morning practice and at other regular services, I experienced the chanting of the Enmei Jukku Kanangyo, the Ten Sutra chant for protecting life, which by the way is part of our services, but only three of our five morning services, so most of you probably never chanted that chant or heard the Mokugyo.
I was really taken by the drumming and the kind of pace of the presentation and puzzled why I got faster and faster towards the ending.

Next, during one of the evening dinners, I sat with an older woman who I hadn't met before and it turns out it was Zenkei Blanche Hartman, who it turns out her image is at our entering altar, a guiding spirit for our practice.
She's the primary Zen sewing teacher and subsequently the first female abbot of the Zen Center.

During that dinner, she asked me where I was from and I told her the Skagit Valley and she said, "Oh, you must go up and visit the Sangha at Red Cedar in Bellingham," which I did, and I kept coming back ever since.

The third thing that happened, apropos of this morning's offering, is one afternoon I saw Monk Amaral and she asked me if I'd like to sit with her and Zenkei Blanche, her teacher, in the Buddha Hall and chant the Enmei Jukku Kanangyo with the magical Mokugyo, which we did for some period of time.
I do know it was more than seven times, which is the usual time we chanted in our services.
It was probably more than 21 times, but I know we chanted for a long time.
I can report that I felt the spirit of that sutra deeply entering my body.
I'm startled in retrospect when I realized that this experience preceded my formal practice that began after I came to Red Cedar.
That foundational moment was then cultivated at Forest Street, where we were before here, before Cedarwood, that included services incorporating the sutra.
At a certain point, I volunteered to be Kokyo, where I had the joy to leave this devotion that furthered my interest and embodiment of its message.

I began to chant it to myself in many different circumstances, whether it was out hiking in the forest or climbing a set of stairs or standing in line at the grocery store, until it has become part of my daily life without prompting or schedule, in the mode of Dogen's continual practice.
One day, hiking on Mount Erie, four lines crystallized in a rhythm that echoed the [unclear: "sign of Japanese"].
The last four lines of the chant are
My little traveling kit includes a small Buddha amulet gifted by Shuko E.D.
Norton, a Japanese small bronze dragon, and a small wooden Kanzeon that I found at a junk store in Hawaii that fits perfectly inside a San Francisco Zen Center incense box.
A small, wooden, slightly curved, delicately balanced image that unless set perfectly straight won't stand up.
She, he is with me wherever I travel, and at home I have other figures of Kuan Yin to accompany my meditation.

On my home altar, I have this four-armed figure who represents one of the images of Kuan Yin I'll speak to in a few minutes, the thousand-armed or infinite-armed Kanzeon holding a few and by implication many, many tools.
In this case, they're only four-armed, just as an example.
Kuan Yin is with me and in me constantly.

With her presence, I am continually reminded of the opportunity to offer assistance in many different ways in the moment-by-moment circumstances which arise in my life, and in that sense arise in each of our lives with each breath we take.

The others who have preceded me in these series of talks about the six perfections and the perfection of generosity, morality, tolerance, patience, energy, meditation, and wisdom have presented various personal views of how one or many of these perfections have entered their lives.

One of my readings in preparing for this talk was the six perfections, Buddhism and the Cultivation of Character by Dale Wright, who [unclear: "Talyssa"] spoke about at some length, both frustrating and appreciative.

Wright proposes that if there is a purpose to our practice or a philosophy of practice, it's of deliberately shaping the kind of life we wish to live and shaping how we respond to the opportunities each moment presents in this life.
It is continuous training in the way we use the word practice, say of a physician, as a continuing effort constantly encountering new challenges and ways to understand the bestness of this moment.

It's very helpful that he looks upon the word perfection to remind us that our studies and considerations are not goals to achieve or ideals to reach, but rather they offer various ways and opportunities of training ourselves to be more open, receptive, and patient in response to the suffering and needs we encounter each moment, whether they are external or internal.
The ultimate aim of these practices, particularly giving, is to cultivate and encourage our compassion, what Wright calls a particular form of human excellence.
Without constant attention and diligence, our tendencies toward greed, possessiveness, hate, and delusion will distort our awareness of and relationship with our interpenetrated reality.
Consistent with Suzuki Roshi, Wright proposes that our training and practicing generosity, for instance, is enlightenment.
Practice is the path, and the path is enlightenment.
Just moving along this path of self-cultivation by developing the six paramitas is the very meaning of enlightenment.
But this is not self-improvement.
In the consumer-based cultural way, we are bombarded with every day.
This is not making ourselves better in some image of who we think we are, or who we think we could, should, or ought to be.

No, this is a practice directed towards more finely honing ourselves to help others, assist others across in small or perhaps large ways, to the other shore of non-obstruction, a recognition of our impermanence, moving along the path of bodhicitta that requires constant effort.
There's no final outcome, no moment where, "Ah, I've gotten there."
Nor does it allow us to forget that our path is continually evolving, changing, and responding to the moment at hand.

One of the characteristics of Buddhism is that it provides us numerous images, whether the Buddha, Manjushri, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteshvara, to provide a physical sense that these perfections occur in this physical samsara world.

For us in Zen Buddhism, and in Buddhism generally, the most prominent bodhisattva image is of Kanzeon, she who sees the suffering of the world, the figure of compassion, and in that sense of generosity, non-judgmental, unqualified, unlimited, and boundless, whether for the infant child or the most hardened criminal, is accepted with all his or her faults.

In our Zen literature, there are collections of pithy stories called koans with commentaries and accompanying verses that help us appreciate in our own ways our understanding of selflessness, impermanence, emptiness, and the interpenetration of all phenomena.
A koan about bodhisattva responsiveness and skillful means, upaya, occurs in three of these volumes, which itself is a statement of how seminal and important her figure is.
The Blue Cliff Record, Case 89, Ungan's "The Whole Body is Hands and Eyes," and the Book of Serenity, Case 54, Yunyan's "Great Compassion."
Dogen also includes this koan in his 300 koan collection, The True Dharma Eye, Case 105, "The Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion."
The text in all three volumes is essentially the same story.
This koan has two characters, Yunyan and Dawu, who, depending on the story, were senior and junior teachers or brothers, but certainly close Dharma companions.
Yunyan asked Dawu, "How does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, Avalokiteshvara, use so many hands and eyes?"
Dawu said, "It's just like a person in the middle of the night, reaching back in search of a pillow."
Yunyan said, "I understand."
Dawu said, "How do you understand it?"
Yunyan said, "All over the body are hands and eyes."
Dawu said, "What you said is roughly all right, but it's only 80 percent."
Yunyan said, "Senior brother, how do you understand it?"
Dawu said, "Throughout the body are hands and eyes."
Two key issues.
First, the effortless and thoughtless reaching for the pillow.
No thinking, no consideration of effort.
Unimpeded, unobstructed action.
In the same way, when we reach out to offer dana, whether actively or passively, there is no exertion, no effort.
How can we see in the dark and know where the invisible is located?
One of the characteristics of a practitioner in the Bodhisattva way is to operate within a universe where the five senses operate as one entity.
Eyes and hands.
Are there other organs?
There is no obstruction and hindering among the sense receptors.
Some commentators assert "all over" or "throughout" are both mental constructs.
Giving is an open tube.
How can we train ourselves to act beyond the divided body?
One commentary says, "If your whole body were an eye, you still wouldn't be able to see it.
If your whole body were an ear, you still wouldn't be able to hear it.
If your whole body were a mouth, you still wouldn't be able to speak it.
And if your whole body were mind, you still wouldn't be able to perceive it."
Because the activity of the Bodhisattva of great compassion is her whole body and mind itself.
It is not limited to any notion or idea.
Yourself or others asking the question in the first place, says one commentator, is a thousand miles from the truth.
Answering only serves to compound this error.
This is reminiscent of the line from the Heart Sutra that in the perfection of wisdom, there is no knowledge and no attainment.
One aspect of viewing this koan is that if we are thinking about hands and eyes, if we are thinking about compassion, then we are still removed from its deliverance.
True dana is free of obstruction, free of mental processes, mentation, free of self-consciousness.

Buddha's teachings have always recognized that the senses defined as individual senses are an illusion, and that all of our senses are constantly working together in one body and one moment to respond to what arises.
I've always been fond of a line by the poet Charles Olson where he says, "We do what we know before we know what we do."
An outcome of our practice that we can experience is that our body is capable of doing things before thought enters into the equation.
That our bodies respond before we know that our bodies are responding.

When we avoid, say, a splinter coming towards our eye, or when we're driving, we turn from a pothole before we think through that we need to turn away from that pothole because it will hurt our tire or cause an accident.
This is doing what we know before we know what we do.

This notion of hands and eyes, either as external elements, as it were, or internally driven by internal elements, is still in the realm of thinking about and not allowing our response to organically address the situation at hand.
Who is grabbing that pillow?
Giving empty of the thought of giving is not an aspect of our being in samsara.
It is fundamental to our being alive.
It comes from our deepest core, Dogen's marrow.
Our teacher, Zoketsu Norman Fish's teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman, whose picture I believe is in the front hall as well, always talked about viewing the other side.
So let me give you two little aspects of other sides of dana.
A curious fact about our vocabulary and understanding is that when we hear the word dana translated as generosity, we immediately imagine something given to another.
Whether it's food to address hunger, money to address poverty, a shoulder to cry on, or the dharma itself to address one's spiritual needs.
The Buddha tells us, "Do give gifts, for poverty is a painful thing.
One is unable when poor to accomplish one's own welfare, much less that of others."
In the iconography, each of Kannon's tool-bearing arms has an eye on the palm and implicitly an ear, tongue, and nose as well.
Wright makes an important point addressing how to use skillful means for meaningful and effective generosity.
He proposes that the first skill for generosity is an effective practice of receptivity.
This is certainly evidenced in the multi-armed presence of Kannon.
How can we know what others need unless we listen to, hear, and see their needs?
This is where our growing instinct and training towards generosity merges with the perfections of wisdom and patience.
Kannon's open arms are invitational and also capable.
Our ability to manifest generosity is really a function of how open we are to others' situation and needs, and how we communicate our openness to them.
In the realm of dana, reciprocity is a key dynamic.
Our generosity expresses our sensitivity and opens our minds to the possibility that someone may need our assistance.
In turn, they may signal their appreciation for this gesture towards them, or not.
Our offer is never contingent or dependent on expected positive feedback.
There's another side of dana we don't often address.
The poet Alan Ginsberg, a deeply devout Buddhist, wrote a Kannon-inspired poem called "Who Be Kind To?"
So many suffering, so many in such need.
Just as Kannon finally thought he had overcome suffering, he realized it kept continually emerging from our human condition.
His head blew apart and was reassembled with nine faces crowned by a three-faced image with a Buddha on top to continue her effort.
With so many in need, who should one be kind to?
Ginsberg's open response is, be kind to yourself.
*It is only one and perishable of many on the planet.

Thou art that one who wishes a soft finger tracing the line of feeling.* In our dedication to others' well-being, we can neglect to maintain our own ability to offer our dana in a full-hearted and focused way.
A quick story.
One evening, speaking to a Zen colleague, struggling with her daughter's profound problems with alcoholism, which had been going on for some time, these lines from Ginsberg popped up.

She had really hit a wall and was clearly burned out from her continuing efforts to assist and her continuing mindfulness about how she might or could possibly do to change the outcome of her daughter's addictive illness.
It struck me that this question was really an important one to ask.
Really, how can you help your daughter if you're totally exhausted of your own resources, don't have the ability to get out of your bed in the morning and continue in the most effective way?
What is the most appropriate way for you to try to support your daughter and also protect and nurture yourself to be of service ahead?
For her, this was a kind of breakthrough, a recognition that she had to take care of herself in order to respond skillfully.
If not, then she couldn't offer her fullest gifts of compassion and concern to assist her child's path towards stability and recovery.
In telling this story, I realized that my dana of advice led to a renewed generosity towards herself and her daughter that might not have manifested otherwise.
Each gesture of generosity furthers the stream of non-obstruction and openness.
It's kind of the Buddhist version of a perpetual motion machine.
An important note in Zoketsu's daily generosity exercises, "In the world could be otherwise," is, quote, "Do something every day for your health and well-being: meditation, exercise, healthy diet."
So remember, be kind to yourself.
Your best efforts are needed each breath.
[unclear: "Pagan"] Leighton's book reminds us that we experience bodhisattvas and their selfless generosity on at least three explicit levels.
The first is the mythic presentation, such as the thousand kanons in a hall that John Wiley and Hannah Sullivan and I experienced in Nara.
I can't remember if it was a thousand, but there were a lot.
Each one was different, each fully embodied and larger than life.

Or the 15-foot-tall, single-tree cypress kuanyin at Hasadera we visited, carved, it is told, in one night out of this huge cedar log, her big toe smooth to a mirror finish by generations of loving fingers.

The second level are those living humans whose pictures grace the book's cover and who we all recognize as exemplary beings who selflessly gave their lives fully to alleviate suffering in the human universe: Mother Teresa, Martin Luther King, Albert Schweitzer, Muhammad Ali.
The third level are those ordinary humans who succor suffering, build community, and forge beneficial relationships that endure long after their last breath.
You don't have to be a Buddhist to be a bodhisattva.
I'll finish these comments with an excerpt from remarks I offered early in February at my cousin Herman's memorial service, whose name we chanted this morning.
In 1995, he was recognized as Rhode Island Philanthropist of the Year.
He provided a significant contribution for this hall we're sitting in right now and many other causes.
I'm honored to recognize his selfless character.
Here's a little excerpt from that talk.
*In Buddhist teachings, there's a constellation of values or perfections that we try to bring forth in our day-to-day life as compassionate humans.
The first of those perfections is generosity.
Many teachers believe that all the other character values from energy to wisdom to patience are contained in and are furthered by generosity.
The spirit of open giving and responding to the ills, misfortunes, and joys we continually live within.*
*Herman Rose had a profound and quizzical understanding about the transience of all of this and approached it all right to the end with a measured equilibrium and a whimsical chuckle.
He gave prudently, strategically, and thoughtfully, but giving wasn't something that he did as a responsibility or as a way to assuage guilt or heal some moral lapse.
No, he didn't do giving, he was giving, right down to the marrow.
It flowed through him naturally, and in his Boy Scout fashion, he tried to leave a place better than he found it, never seeking recognition, quietly and simply getting the work done.
Leaving things better for and between all kinds of people and for the practice, places they live, work, and raise their kids.*
Now, we'll finish up by embodying the spirit of Kanzeon, and we'll chant together this Dharani-like sutra for protecting and sustaining life.
So, grab that mokugyo.
You can do it, yeah.
We'll do it seven times.
I was going to turn it on, but we'll do it seven times, because we'll have some time for talk.

*Enmei, juku, kanangyo, butsuyo, butsuyo, butsuyo, kugajo, chonen, Kanzeon, boushin, ishin, Kanzeon, butsuyo, butsuyo, butsuyo, butsuyo, kanjyo, bonen, Kanzeon, nenen, jushin, butsuyo, butsuyo, butsuyo, jo, akugajo, chonen, Kanzeon, bonen, Kanzeon, nenen, jushin, kinen, Kanzeon, butsuyo, butsuyo,*
I think we have a few minutes.
How are we doing for time given, what?
So maybe we should do this as a group as a whole rather than breaking down into a small group.
A couple of questions posed to me thinking about this talk and its conclusion.
Three questions.
How can I get out of my own way to offer a dana without reluctance or fear?
What do I hold onto when opportunity for a dana arises in my life?
And at what point am I uncomfortable with offering something of value?
What would be the harm to myself, the benefit to another?
So, a kind of cluster of questions about what keeps us from opening, freely opening, without precondition and without expectation.
And so I open up to the floor for response, to think that through a little bit.
